♻ ☆ RMRRT: Riemannian Barrier Metric RRT for Inequality-Aware Steering on Equality Manifolds
Minhyeong Kang, Sanghyun Kim
This paper presents a motion planning framework that unifies equality and inequality constraints within a single geometric formulation for sampling-based planning in high-dimensional robotic systems. In conventional sampling-based planners, equality constraints are typically enforced through projection, whereas inequality constraints are handled separately through binary validity checks such as collision testing, often leading to inefficient exploration. To address this limitation, we propose Riemannian Barrier Metric RRT (RMRRT), which constructs a unified local geometry for planning on equality-constrained manifolds. RMRRT first builds an ambient barrier metric from inequality-sensitive barrier terms and then induces a tangent-space metric via a G-orthogonal projection associated with the equality constraints. The resulting tangent-space metric is used consistently in both steering and nearest-neighbor selection, biasing exploration away from nearby inequality boundaries while preserving first-order equality consistency. In this work, the metric is instantiated from signed-distance-based geometric proxy inequalities to provide collision-informative tangent-space directions; hard feasibility is enforced separately through standard validity checks. Experimental results show that RMRRT achieves a 100% success rate across diverse constrained manipulation tasks in both simulation and real-world settings, while reducing planning time relative to representative constrained planning baselines. Ablation studies further demonstrate that the proposed metric improves exploration quality by reducing rejected samples and shortening path length. Experiment videos and source code are available at: https://rcilab.khu.ac.kr/rmrrt/
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures, 8 tables. Accepted to IEEE Transactions on Robotics (T-RO). Project page: https://rcilab.khu.ac.kr/rmrrt/
♻ ☆ Depth-Only Open-Vocabulary 3D Semantic Segmentation For Privacy-Preserving Robotic Applications WACV
Xuying Huang, Sicong Pan, Maren Bennewitz
Privacy-preserving perception is increasingly important for robotic systems operating in real-world indoor environments, yet it remains underexplored in open-vocabulary 3D semantic segmentation. We study this problem under an RGB-prohibited deployment setting motivated by scene-specific visual information disclosure, where real RGB observations are unavailable during scene acquisition and fusion. To reflect this deployment constraint on existing 3D datasets, we adopt a stricter depth-only evaluation protocol that re-runs scene fusion without RGB and exposes only the resulting depth-derived geometry to the segmentation pipeline. This constraint removes appearance cues that are often critical for open-vocabulary recognition, making depth-only predictions more uncertain and less reliable. To address this challenge, we propose UTTO, a model-agnostic uncertainty-guided test-time optimization framework that uses structured predictive uncertainty as a reliability signal to refine predictions from frozen open-vocabulary 3D backbones. Experiments across ScanNet and Matterport3D demonstrate consistent improvements over multiple depth-only backbones. Privacy recoverability analyses and a real-robot semantic goal grounding case study further support the proposed privacy-constrained setting and applicability.

☆ Statistical, Machine Learning and Deep Learning Methods for Missing Covariates: An Empirical Evaluation with Applications to Alzheimer's Disease Research
Yiqing Pan, Sharon X. Xie, Shujie Ma, Angela L. Jefferson, Panpan Zhang
Missing data are common in biomedical research, particularly when biomarkers are costly or require invasive procedures to obtain, such as cerebrospinal fluid measures in Alzheimer's disease. Although a wide range of missing data methods exists, from traditional statistical approaches to modern machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms, their comparative performance under different missingness mechanisms remains insufficiently understood. In this study, we provide an empirical evaluation of eight methods for handling missing covariates, including complete-case analysis, multiple imputation, ML-based techniques, and DL frameworks such as multilayer perceptrons, variational autoencoders, and generative adversarial networks. We summarize their conceptual foundations, practical implementation considerations, strengths, and limitations. Through extensive simulations, we assess estimation bias, efficiency, standard error accuracy, confidence interval coverage, and computational burden across different missingness mechanisms and proportions. An application to the Vanderbilt Memory and Aging Project further illustrates the implications of different methods for regression analysis in a real-world biomedical setting. Finally, we provide practical recommendations for method selection and highlight remaining challenges that warrant future investigation.
☆ The low-degree sample complexity of clustering Gaussian mixtures with more groups than dimensions
Alexandra Carpentier, Nicolas Verzelen
We study the computational limits of clustering $n$ observations drawn from a mixture of $K$ isotropic Gaussian distributions in $\mathbb R^d$, when the number $K$ of groups is much larger than the dimension $d$. In this regime, distance-based and spectral procedures require a squared separation $Δ^2$ of order $\sqrt d$. In contrast, tensor-based procedures cluster at a polylogarithmic separation but need a sample size that is a large polynomial of $dK$, and the low-degree lower bounds known for random centers only show that $n$ must exceed $dK^2$. Focusing on normally distributed centers, we characterize the minimal separation for clustering with low-degree polynomials in the regime $K>d$, through a low-degree lower bound and a matching upper bound, up to subpolynomial factors. In particular, for $K=d^{p/2}$ with $p> 2$ a real number, we show that a sample size of the order of $K^3 d^{(\lceil p\rceil-p)/2}$ is required to recover the clustering with subpolynomial separation, and that it suffices when $p$ is not an integer.
☆ HapBO: Harnessed $α$-$π$ Bayesian Optimization via Expert Natural Language Priors
Jean-Sébastien Giroux, Rose Guay Hottin, Marco Bonizzato
Bayesian Optimization (BO) can be substantially more sample-efficient when informed by prior knowledge about the problem. In practice, however, such knowledge is often available only in natural language, e.g., expert intuitions or documentation, rather than as the explicit probability distribution landscape that prior-guided BO methods may require. Leveraging it effectively demands both an expressive mapping from language to priors and robustness to information that may be misleading. We propose HapBO (Harnessed $α$-$π$ Bayesian Optimization), which elicits beliefs once from a human expert, a large language model (LLM), or both, and deterministically compiles a structured specification into a reusable belief function ($π: \mathcal{X} \to[0,1]$), with a rich representation not restricted to a Gaussian family. Building on $α$-$π$BO, HapBO applies this belief function through a bounded positive multiplier on any nonnegative acquisition, preserving positive acquisition support and requiring no LLM calls during optimization. We prove that, for the Expected Improvement acquisition function (EI), HapBO preserves the standard simple-regret rate up to a bounded factor, even under adversarial beliefs. We evaluate HapBO on 40 HPOBench tasks, a synthetic suite in 6-15 dimensions and two real-world applications: cortical neurostimulation and constrained solar design. HapBO achieves the lowest aggregate HPOBench regret and strong real-world task performance, with zero in-loop token cost. In real-world applications it improves the optimization outcome even at budgets of 12-20 queries, and at a small fraction of the wall-clock and token costs of other LLM-based methods.
comment: 41 pages, 22 figures, 8 tables. Code: https://github.com/mbonizzato/HapBO
☆ Empirical Variational Bayes Factorization for Longitudinal Matrix Data
Jiakun Li, Eric F. Lock
Collecting high-dimensional data over time for multiple individuals is increasingly common in biomedical research, particularly in studies of disease progression or molecular time-course experiments. Often data are missing or the timepoints are irregularly spaced across individuals. There is a lack of flexible methodology to explore latent patterns of change over time and account for missing data. We propose an empirical variational Bayes (EVB) approach to factorize high-dimensional longitudinal data, in which the underlying factors have temporal correlation over time. The EVB approach is computationally efficient and accommodates flexible covariance structures over time with automatic determination of all hyper-parameters (including the underlying rank, i.e., number of factors). Simulations demonstrate that the approach captures the underlying signal more precisely than other strategies, and performs well with respect to missing data imputation under different scenarios. An application to a gene time-course data for multiple sclerosis treatment provides a factorization with interpretable components over time and improved imputation accuracy for missing data.

☆ Near-Quadratic Sample Compression for All VC Classes
Yang Cai, Vineet Gupta, Yanchen Jiang, Christopher Liaw, Aranyak Mehta, Shay Moran, Grigoris Velegkas, Di Wang, Manfred K. Warmuth
The sample compression conjecture is a longstanding open problem in learning theory, originating in the work of Littlestone and Warmuth in the 1980s. At its heart is a connection between simplification and generalization: if a predictor consistent with a training sample is defined using only a small part of that sample, then it is likely to generalize. Sample compression schemes formalize this idea, and many natural learning algorithms can be analyzed this way. The sample compression conjecture of Floyd and Warmuth (1995) asserts that every binary concept class of VC dimension $d$ admits a sample compression scheme of size $O(d)$; a weaker conjecture asks only for size polynomial in $d$. Both have remained open: the first bound depending only on $d$, due to Moran and Yehudayoff (2016), is exponential in $d$. We prove the weaker conjecture by constructing a sample compression scheme of size $O(d^2 \log^2 d)$.
☆ Decomposing SGD Dynamics in Neural Networks: Teacher-Induced Spikes and Variance Inflation NeurIPS 2026
Samet Demir, Zafer Dogan
We study two-layer neural networks trained by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on a multi-index teacher model, focusing on how first-layer parameters orthogonal to the teacher subspace affect generalization. We decompose the first-layer weights into a signal component aligned with the teacher and an orthogonal complement, and analyze their joint SGD dynamics together with the second layer in the proportional limit. We show that although SGD updates to the complement are initially isotropic, the training dynamics induce teacher-dependent spectral spikes in the complement Gram matrix. This emergent anisotropy provides a concrete mechanism by which representation variance is amplified, and generalization degrades. To isolate this effect, we introduce Decomposed Dynamics, an analytically tractable surrogate whose asymptotic test-error dynamics coincide with those of SGD. In simulations with a ReLU student, freezing the directions of the orthogonal complement improves generalization relative to training them. Finally, we show that the signal component rapidly aligns with the second-layer weights, revealing strong cross-layer coupling even in this shallow setting. Together, our results provide a dynamical explanation for how feature learning outside the teacher subspace harms generalization.

☆ Equivariant Modeling with Polynomial Features via Minimal Homogeneous Generators
Michael Liaofan Liu, Joe Kileel
We present a general framework for modeling and learning equivariant functions between finite dimensional semisimple real group representations, unifying constructions developed across many application areas. Our model is a linear combination of equivariant polynomial features whose coefficients are arbitrary learnable functions of invariant polynomial features. We take as features minimal homogeneous generators for the invariant algebra and the covariant module over the invariant algebra, up to prescribed degrees. We provide a Python package that automatically computes these features and fits the resulting models to training data. The algorithm for feature computation requires explicit isotypic decompositions of the input and output representations, along with explicit Clebsch-Gordan decompositions of the tensor product of irreducible representations, and achieves speedups over alternative methods in computational algebra. Numerical experiments in scientific modeling demonstrate the full learning pipeline and yield accurate predictors with few trainable parameters, using the model both for end-to-end prediction and within layers of larger architectures.
♻ ☆ Information Theory and Statistical Learning
Abbas El Gamal
This manuscript contains preprint of a chapter in the forthcoming third edition of Cover and Thomas's Elements of Information Theory, posted with permission from Wiley. For feedback, please contact abbas@ee.stanford.edu. Learning and information theory intersect in both model training and the characterization of fundamental performance limits. This manuscript provides a concise and accessible treatment of the first intersection, requiring only basic background in information theory and statistics at the senior undergraduate / first-year graduate level. End-of-chapter exercises make the material well suited for classroom use as well as self-study. The chapter focuses on the role of divergence measures in model training, with examples ranging from linear and logistic regression to autoregressive models, variational autoencoders, diffusion models, and score-based models. In particular, the treatment of the generative diffusion model provides a more systematic and explicit derivation than is typical in the literature.
♻ ☆ On the Complexity of Offline Reinforcement Learning with Q*-Approximation and Partial Coverage
Haolin Liu, Braham Snyder, Chen-Yu Wei
We study offline reinforcement learning under $Q^\star$-approximation and partial coverage, a setting that motivates practical algorithms such as Conservative $Q$-Learning (CQL; Kumar et al., 2020) but has received limited theoretical attention. Our work is inspired by the following open question: "Are $Q^\star$-realizability and Bellman completeness sufficient for sample-efficient offline RL under partial coverage?" We answer in the negative via an information-theoretic lower bound. To identify additional structure that enables sample-efficient offline RL under partial coverage, we introduce a general decision-estimation framework, inspired by model-free decision-estimation coefficients (DEC) for online RL (Foster et al., 2023b; Liu et al., 2025b). Our framework decomposes offline RL complexity into decision complexity and value estimation error. This allows modular study of both sub-problems. Our result not only unifies existing results (Chen and Jiang, 2022; Uehara et al., 2023), but further improves and generalizes them. On the decision complexity side, our improvement includes: the first $ε^{-2}$ sample complexity bound for soft $Q$-learning under partial coverage that improves Uehara et al.'s (2023) $ε^{-4}$ bound, the removal of the need for additional online interaction in the value-gap setting of Chen and Jiang (2022), and new learnable settings beyond the above two cases. On the value estimation side, we provide a new characterization of the role of Bellman completeness under partial coverage, and the first characterization of offline learnability for general low-Bellman-rank MDPs (Jiang et al., 2017; Du et al., 2021; Jin et al., 2021). The latter is a canonical online RL setting that has remained unexplored in offline RL except for special cases. As a side contribution, our techniques give the first analysis of CQL in the function approximation setting.
♻ ☆ Omni-modal decomposition autoencoders learn full-stack wearable disentangled representations
Ioannis Ziogas, Ensieh Khazaei, Bilal Taha, Aamna Al Shehhi, Ahsan H. Khandoker, Leontios J. Hadjileontiadis, Dimitrios Hatzinakos
Learning disentangled representations is key for general-purpose multi-modal wearable models, yet existing approaches rarely combine classification, disentanglement, fusion, and generation of heterogeneous multi-modal time series in a single model. We introduce Omni-modal Variational Decomposition Autoencoders (OmniDecVAEs), a framework that learns multi-purpose representations from arbitrarily many modalities with a single shared encoder-decoder. OmniDecVAEs extend DecVAEs by learning time-frequency latent subspaces per modality through a multi-view self-supervised decomposition loss and a component-wise conditional decoder. On the omni-modal human activity recognition (HAR) HARWE dataset (up to thirty channels) and the public UCI HAR and WESAD datasets, OmniDecVAEs learn the most disentangled representations for unseen subjects (DCI disentanglement up to 3.0 percentage points (pp) higher). On HARWE, they improve subject-dependent HAR and identity recognition by 1.1 pp and 5.8 pp, and outperform supervised end-to-end models by +31.6 pp and +22.3 pp on unseen subjects of multi-device datasets. Moreover, their generative capacity improves reconstruction mean squared error over multi-modal VAEs (34-74% improvement) and their synthetic data improve affect recognition on unseen subjects (2 pp). With 4.1M parameters, invariant to the number of modalities (21xfewer than a multi-branch VAE), OmniDecVAEs are scalable, single-model full-stack learners for wearable representations.
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, 7 tables
♻ ☆ Active Learning For Contextual Linear Optimization: A Margin-Based Approach
Mo Liu, Paul Grigas, Heyuan Liu, Zuo-Jun Max Shen
We develop the first active learning method for contextual linear optimization. Specifically, we introduce a label acquisition algorithm that sequentially decides whether to request the ``labels'' of feature samples arriving in an unlabeled data stream, where the labels correspond to the objective coefficients in the linear optimization problem. The label acquisition rule is guided by the decision loss induced by the predicted coefficients, known as the Smart Predict-then-Optimize (SPO) loss. Motivated by the structure of the SPO loss, our algorithm uses the distance to degeneracy as a margin-based criterion for label acquisition. The algorithm processes incoming feature samples in batches, acquiring within each batch only the labels of samples whose distance to degeneracy falls below a rejection threshold. We derive non-asymptotic bounds for direct SPO-loss minimization over a general hypothesis class and for surrogate-loss minimization over a linear prediction class. These bounds demonstrate that, under certain natural conditions, our margin-based active learning algorithm requires fewer labels than supervised learning to achieve the same excess population risk for the chosen training loss. We provide concrete examples in which these conditions hold under continuous (sub-)Gaussian noise. Finally, we present numerical evidence demonstrating the practical value of our approach in applications such as personalized pricing and shortest-path problems.
♻ ☆ Wedge Sampling: Efficient Tensor Completion with Nearly-Linear Sample Complexity
Hengrui Luo, Anna Ma, Ludovic Stephan, Yizhe Zhu
We introduce wedge sampling, a non-adaptive sampling scheme for recovering an order-$k$ low-rank tensor of side length $n$ from structured observations of its entries. The scheme samples pairs of entries in the same column of a tensor unfolding, forming length-two paths (wedges) in the associated bipartite sampling graph. The products of the paired entries supply the row correlations needed for spectral initialization in regimes where uniform sampling yields too few wedges. For fixed rank, incoherence, tensor order, and condition number, wedge sampling enables polynomial-time recovery with nearly linear sample complexity in $n$. The spectral initializer can be combined with existing refinement procedures using only an additional $\tilde O(n)$ uniformly sampled entries. Spectral refinement achieves weak recovery to any fixed relative Frobenius error. For symmetric third-order tensors with incoherent canonical polyadic factors, gradient descent achieves exact recovery in the noiseless setting, with error decreasing geometrically. The improvement over the $\tilde O(n^{k/2})$ sample complexity typical of efficient methods under uniform entry sampling shows how the conjectured computational barrier depends on the observation model. A key ingredient for the gradient descent analysis is a concentration bound for sparse random tensors in an incoherent spectral norm. We also give error bounds for both procedures under additive Gaussian noise and explicit signal-to-noise conditions. Beyond tensor completion, the same sampling scheme improves the sample complexity of one-sided matrix completion, where the goal is to recover the left singular subspace of a matrix with many more columns than rows.
comment: 87 pages, 5 figures. Includes sharpened noiseless guarantees
♻ ☆ Prior-Amortized In-Context Bayesian Inference for Generalized Linear Mixed-Effects Models
Alex Kipnis, Marcel Binz, Eric Schulz
Hierarchical data is ubiquitous in the empirical sciences and most commonly analyzed with generalized linear mixed-effects models (GLMMs). Bayesian inference for GLMMs yields calibrated uncertainty estimates but requires Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). The gold-standard No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) is slow and must restart from scratch for every new dataset, model and prior specification. We introduce MetaBeta, a pretrained amortized model for in-context Bayesian inference over GLMMs. The full prior and model specification are supplied as context at test time, and the model returns an asymptotically exact posterior at the speed of a forward pass. Two set transformers and two conditional neural spline flows mirror the GLMM's hierarchical structure and are trained jointly on millions of realistic simulated datasets with continuous, binary and count outcomes. The flow posterior is refined by Independence Metropolis-Hastings against the unnormalized posterior. This yields tuning-free asymptotically correct inference. Alternatively, MetaBeta can warm-start NUTS. This gives nearly identical inference 3.5-13x faster than cold-started NUTS and removes over 98% of NUTS' divergent transitions. On controlled benchmarks with ground-truth parameters, MetaBeta matches NUTS in parameter recovery, posterior calibration and out-of-sample prediction. On real datasets with unknown parameters, priors and model structure, its posteriors closely agree with those of NUTS. Furthermore, it remains faithful where amortized models typically struggle: under misspecified likelihoods, misspecified priors, out-of-distribution predictors, collinear designs and data-poor regimes. On real data, a full prior sensitivity analysis including model comparison takes a few seconds with MetaBeta against 14-18 core-hours for NUTS, tracing its posteriors throughout. Our model is open-source and open-weights.
♻ ☆ Bigger Isn't Always Memorizing: Early Stopping Overparameterized Diffusion Models
Alessandro Favero, Antonio Sclocchi, Matthieu Wyart
Diffusion probabilistic models have become a cornerstone of modern generative AI, yet the mechanisms underlying their generalization remain poorly understood. In fact, if these models were perfectly minimizing their training loss, they would just generate data belonging to their training set, i.e., memorize, as empirically found in the overparameterized regime. We revisit this view by showing that, in highly overparameterized diffusion models, generalization in natural data domains is progressively achieved during training before the onset of memorization. Our results, ranging from image to language diffusion models, systematically support the empirical law that memorization time is proportional to the dataset size, consistent with a kernel-regression bound on the time required to fit the empirical score at low noise. Generalization vs. memorization is then best understood as a competition between time scales. We show that this phenomenology is recovered in diffusion models learning a simple probabilistic context-free grammar with random rules, where generalization corresponds to the hierarchical acquisition of deeper grammar rules as training time grows, and the generalization cost of early stopping can be characterized. We summarize these results in a phase diagram. Overall, our results support that a principled early-stopping criterion - scaling with dataset size - can effectively optimize generalization while avoiding memorization, with direct implications for hyperparameter transfer and privacy-sensitive applications.
♻ ☆ From Data to Action: Accelerating Refinery Optimization with AI
Dániel Pfeifer, Ábrahám Papp, Tibor Bernáth, Tamás Zoltán Varga, Márk Czifra, Botond Szilágyi, Edith Alice Kovács
Nowadays refinery optimization utilizes sheer amounts of data, which can be handled with modern Linear Programming (LP) software, but the interpreting and applying the results remains challenging. Large petrochemical companies use massive models, with hundreds of thousands of input matrix elements. The LP solution is mathematically correct, but simplifications are made in the model, and data supply errors may occur. Therefore, further insight is needed to trust the results. The novelty of the paper consists of enhancing the LP solver with a memory, which makes possible to find potential errors in the input data, finding unusual relations in the data on different decision levels, by introducing an anomaly detection tool. Analyzing the potential "anomalies" in the input and output of LP, the subsequent LP solutions can be improved. The Anomaly Detection tool proposed comprises three methodologies. A transformed version of the popular ECOD methodology is applied. New methods are proposed to handle high-dimensional data: choosing the most informative pairs. Then, this is used alongside two 2D Anomaly Detection algorithms, revealing several business opportunities and data supply errors in the MOL refinery scheduling and planning architecture. The proposed tool learns connections in past data and runs very efficiently on present data revealing unusual connections sorted by their importance. Up to this step, optimization and Anomaly Detection happened automatically, and thereafter, decision makers may take a look at the most relevant anomalies found, and decide how to further improve the subsequent LPs. The tool also has periodic retraining built in.
comment: 47 pages, 17 figures
♻ ☆ Low-Dimensional Adaptation of Rectified Flow: A Diffusion and Stochastic Localization Perspective
Saptarshi Roy, Alessandro Rinaldo, Purnamrita Sarkar
In recent years, Rectified flow (RF) has gained considerable popularity largely due to its generation efficiency and state-of-the-art performance. In this paper, we investigate how well RF automatically adapts to the intrinsic low dimensionality of the support of the target distribution to accelerate sampling. We show that, using a carefully designed end-point adapted time-discretization scheme and with sufficiently accurate drift estimates, the RF sampler enjoys an iteration complexity of order $O(k/\varepsilon)$ (up to log factors), where $\varepsilon$ is the precision in total variation distance and $k$ is the intrinsic dimension of the target distribution. In addition, we show that the denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) procedure is equivalent to a stochastic version of RF by establishing a novel connection between these processes and stochastic localization. Building on this connection, we further design a stochastic RF sampler that also adapts to the low-dimensionality of the target distribution under mild requirements on the accuracy of the drift estimates, and also with a specific time schedule. We illustrate the efficacy of newly designed time-discretization schedules with simulations on the synthetic data and text-to-image (T2I) data experiments.
